'''Robert Harley''' (23 January 1828 – 26 July 1910) was an English Congregational minister and mathematician.

==Life==
Born in [[Liverpool]] on 23 January 1828, he was third son of Robert Harley by his wife Mary, daughter of William Stevenson, and niece of General Stevenson of [[Ayr]].. The father, after a career as a merchant, became a minister of the [[Wesleyan Methodist Association]]. Harley's mathematical aptitude developed at school in [[Blackburn]] under William Hoole, and age 16 he was appointed to a mathematical mastership at [[Seacombe]], near Liverpool, returning later to teach at Blackburn.<ref name="DNB">{{cite DNB12|wstitle=Harley, Robert|volume=2}}</ref><ref>{{cite ODNB|id=33715|first=Maria|last=Panteki|title=Harley, Robert}}</ref>

He was elected to corresponding membership of the [[Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society]]  on 30 April 1850.<ref> MEMOIRS AND PROCEEDINGS MANCHESTER LITERARY & PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY. Volume LII. (1907-8 </ref>

In 1854 Harley entered the Congregational ministry, and was at [[Brighouse]], Yorkshire, until 1868, after a time also filling the chair of mathematics and logic at [[Airedale College]] from 1864 to 1868.<ref name="WhoWho">{{cite magazine|title=Harley, Rev. Robert|magazine=Who's Who|year=1910|page=856|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015047640100;view=1up;seq=894}}</ref> In 1863 he was admitted [[Fellow of the Royal Society]]. He acted as secretary of the A section of the British Association at meetings at Norwich (1868) and Edinburgh (1871); and was a vice-president of the meetings at Bradford (1873), Bath (1888), and Cardiff (1891).<ref name="DNB"/>

From 1868 to 1872 he was pastor of the oldest Congregational church in [[Leicester]], and from 1872 to 1881 was vice-principal of [[Mill Hill School]], where he officiated in the chapel. At Mill Hill he was instrumental in erecting a public lecture hall for [[total abstinence]] talks as well as popular entertainment and instruction. From 1882 to 1885 he was principal of [[Huddersfield College]], and from 1886 to 1890 minister of the Congregational church in [[Oxford]], where he was made hon. M.A. in 1886.<ref name="DNB"/>

Having taken a ministerial appointment in Australia, Harley was pastor of Heath Church, [[Halifax, West Yorkshire|Halifax]], from 1892 until 1895, when he retired and settled at [[Forest Hill, London|Forest Hill]], near London. He continued to preach in London and the provinces, and as a [[temperance (virtue)|temperance]] advocate.<ref name="DNB"/>

Harley died at Rosslyn, Westbourne Road, Forest Hill, on 26 July 1910, and was buried in [[Ladywell cemetery]].<ref name="DNB"/>

==Works==
Throughout his career mathematics remained a major interest for Harley. He spent time on the [[theory of equations]], especially the theory of the [[general equation of the fifth degree]]. His conclusions, which were published in ''Memoirs of the Manchester Lit. and Phil. Soc'' 1860, xv. 172–219, were independently reached at the same time by [[Sir James Cockle]]. Harley's two further papers on the ''Theory of Quintics''<ref>''Quarterly Journal of Mathematics'' 1860–2, iii. 343–59; v. 248–60</ref> and an exposition of Cockle's method of symmetric products in ''[[Phil. Trans.]]'' (1860) attracted the attention of [[Arthur Cayley]], who carried the research further.<ref name="DNB"/>

Harley failed to complete the treatise on [[Quintic function|quintics]] which he had begun, but continued to publish. A sketch of the life and work of [[George Boole]] appeared in the ''British Quarterly Review'' (July 1866), and a memoir of his friend, Sir James Cockle, is in the ''Proceedings'' of the Royal Society, vol. lix.<ref name="DNB"/>

==Family==
In 1854 Harley married Sara, daughter of James Stroyan of Wigan; she died in 1905.<ref name="DNB"/> Upon his death he was survived by two sons and a daughter.<ref name="WhoWho"/>

Their son Harold Harley (1860–1937), using the pen name [[Mark Ambient]], was a dramatist and librettist of musical comedies.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=Abx6EqTRfqEC&pg=PA246 ''Alumni Cantabrigienses: A Biographical List of All Known Students, Graduates and Holders of Office at the University of Cambridge, from the Earliest Times to 1900''] Volume 2, page 246.</ref><ref>{{cite book|chapter=Ambient, Mark|title=Who's Who in the Theatre|edition=4th|year=1922|page=11|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qyk_AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA11}}</ref>
